course.title: Rust Foundations
course.description: Read, run and write small Rust programs, with the real compiler checking your work.
course.audience: Someone new to Rust. Some programming in another language helps but isn't needed.

paragraphs: Rust is a systems programming language whose compiler examines a program far more thoroughly than most before it will let the program run, and a beginner meets that compiler early and often. This course treats it as a teacher: the programs are short, you say what each one does before running it, and when rustc refuses one, its message shows which rule was broken and usually how to mend it.

The first lesson covers how a program prints values, how a name is attached to a value with let, and why Rust keeps a name unchangeable unless it is declared with mut. The second covers whole and decimal number types, the rule that stops them being mixed by accident, and functions that take and return values of stated types. Every exercise that asks for code is compiled and run for real, and the same tools are open to you in the playground and in the Rust projects.
outcomes: You'll be able to read a short Rust program and say what it prints.
You'll be able to name a value with let and decide whether it may change with mut.
You'll be able to choose between i32 and f64 and predict the result of dividing whole numbers.
You'll be able to write a function with typed parameters and a return type.
introduction.prerequisites: Some programming in another language helps, but nothing beyond everyday arithmetic is assumed.

lessons.title: Print a value, then change it

steps.headline: A Rust program starts at fn main, and println! prints a line of text.

lead.text: Every Rust program that you run begins at a function called **fn main**, whose body is the pair of braces that follows it. The lines inside are carried out in order from the top, and when the last one has finished the program ends, which is why the programs in this lesson share the same outer shape and differ only in what is written between the braces.

The line that produces output is **println!**, which prints its text and then starts a new line. The exclamation mark shows that println! is a *macro* and not an ordinary function, a difference that does not matter yet, and the text it prints is written between double quotation marks. Wherever the text contains a pair of braces, Rust fills the gap with one of the values listed after the text, taking the values in order, so that the first {} receives the first value, the second {} the second, and so on.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the three pairs of braces are filled by 6, 7 and 6 * 7. The last of these was never written out as a number, because Rust works out 6 * 7 before printing, so **any calculation placed after the text is carried out first and its result is printed**. Both the order of the values and this use of a calculation are needed in the next two exercises.

lead.text: The program below prints 2 and 5. Rust fills the braces in the order in which the values are listed, and the exercise is to make the same text come out with the numbers the other way round.

reveal.text: Matching braces to values by position works for two values and becomes tedious for six, which is one reason the next idea is to give each value a name.

lead.text: This time the body of main is empty, so the lines are yours to write. Each println! ends its line, which means that two lines of output need two calls.

steps.headline: let gives a value a name, and later lines can use the name in place of the value.

lead.text: Writing 3 + 4 after the text is enough for a single sum, but a program soon needs the same value in several places, and repeating a number would mean changing every copy whenever the number changed. Rust avoids this by letting you attach a name to a value with **let**: the line let price = 4; creates the name price, gives it the value 4, and from that line onwards price can be written wherever 4 could.

A name can be defined from other names, because the right-hand side of a let is a calculation like any other. In the figure, cost is given the value price * quantity, which Rust works out when it reaches that line, and the final println! then prints all three names. Inside the braces of the text a name may be written directly, as in {cost}, and Rust fills the gap with the value that the name stands for.

afterFigure.text: Each line can use only names that were created *above* it, because the program is carried out from the top and a name that has not yet been created has no value to offer. That is why cost, which depends on price and quantity, comes after both of them. A name made in this way is called a **variable**, although, as the next screens show, in Rust it does not vary unless you ask it to.

lead.text: Read the program from the top, keeping track of the value each name holds, and say what number follows area = in the output before running anything.

reveal.text: Edit the program and run it to check. Changing the 4 in the second line changes the answer without touching any other line, which is the advantage of keeping a value under one name.

lead.text: Line 3 of this program tries to give score a second value with =. Read it as rustc, the Rust compiler, will, and decide whether the compiler accepts it.

reveal.text: The message points at line 3 for the new assignment and at line 2 for the let that created score, because the fault lies in how the name was made. A name created with a plain let is **immutable**: it receives one value and keeps it, so that anyone reading let score = 10; can rely on score being 10 everywhere below that line.

outcome.diagnostics:
error[E0384]: cannot assign twice to immutable variable `score`
 --> main.rs:3:5
  |
2 |     let score = 10;
  |         ----- first assignment to `score`
3 |     score = score + 5;
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ cannot assign twice to immutable variable
  |
help: consider making this binding mutable
  |
2 |     let mut score = 10;
  |         +++

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0384`.

steps.headline: Writing mut after let allows a variable to be given a new value later.

lead.text: The repair that rustc suggested is a single word. Writing the word **mut**, short for *mutable*, after let tells Rust at the moment a name is created that it will be given new values later, and with that permission an assignment such as lives = lives - 1 is accepted. The right-hand side is worked out first from the old value and the result then replaces it, so that after the assignment lives holds 2 and the 3 is gone.

Rust asks for the permission at the start, and not for the change at the moment it happens, for a reason that grows with the size of a program. When every name is unchangeable unless it is marked, a reader can see at once which names are able to change, and the ones without mut can be set aside when hunting for a value that has gone wrong. The cost to the writer is one word.

afterFigure.text: Only the creation of the variable is marked, and only once: the later assignments are plain lines such as lives = lives - 1, with no let and no mut. Writing let again would do something else, which is the subject of the last idea in this lesson.

lead.text: The program from the last question is below, still with its error. The repair touches only one line, and the quickest way to find it is to run the program and read what rustc says.

reveal.text: The edit was made on line 2, where the name is created, and not on line 3, where the change happens: the permission belongs to the let.

steps.headline: A second let with the same name creates a new variable that hides the first.

lead.text: A different value can also arrive under the same name without mut. If a program writes let amount = 4; and later let amount = amount * 3;, the second line is not an assignment to the first amount. It creates a *new* variable that happens to share the name, calculated from the old one, and from that line onwards the name refers to the new variable. This is called **shadowing**, because the new variable casts a shadow over the old one.

Since the second amount is a new variable, nothing obliges it to resemble the first. In the figure it holds the number 12 and then, after a third let, the text twelve, which no assignment to a single variable could do, because an assignment must keep the type of value the variable was created with (the next lesson explains types properly). Shadowing is therefore the tool for building a value in stages, while mut suits a value that is updated again and again in place, such as a counter.

afterFigure.text: Each let leaves the earlier variable unchanged and merely out of reach by name, whereas an assignment overwrites the one variable that exists. When it is unclear which of the two a line is, check whether the line begins with **let**.

lead.text: The program below changes level twice with plain assignments, and rustc rejects both. The repair this time is to shadow level, not to make it mutable.

reveal.text: Both approaches print 7, so the choice between them depends on the job: shadowing when each step produces a fresh value, possibly of another type, and mut when one variable is updated repeatedly.

lessons.orientation: Read and write small programs that print values, and decide which of their variables are allowed to change.
lessons.reviewLabel: Print a value, then change it
lessons.nextAction: Give your values types and put a calculation in a function.

blocks.text: Here is a complete Rust program, and you can probably say what it prints without having been told a single rule of the language. Two names, apples and pears, are each given a number, and the last line writes out something calculated from them.

Some of what you can see will be unfamiliar, such as the exclamation mark after println and the pair of braces, and those details are set out over the next few screens. The larger subject is how a program holds values: a name is attached to a value, the name is used wherever the value is needed, and Rust requires you to say *in advance* which names may change later. That requirement is the first thing that separates Rust from most languages you may have used, and it is the reason the compiler will sometimes refuse a program that looks perfectly reasonable.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to write a program that prints values, and say which of its variables may change.

recap.keyIdea: A name made with let keeps its value unless it was made with let mut, and println! fills its braces with the values or names you give it.

blocks.text: A Rust program starts at fn main, and **println!** fills each pair of braces with the next value, or with a name written inside the braces. A name created with **let** keeps its value, and only one created with **let mut** may be assigned a new one later, whereas a second let with the same name makes a *new* variable and leaves the old one untouched.

For a rejected assignment, rustc's message ends with the repair itself, so running the program is the quickest way to find out what is wrong with it. A name that never needs to change should be left without mut, because the missing word tells every later reader that its value can be trusted, and a [[shadowing|A second let that reuses a name and creates a new variable. Met earlier in this lesson.]] let is the way to build a value in stages when each stage is a new variable.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at the two kinds of number a variable can hold, whole numbers and decimals, and at putting a calculation inside a function of your own.

lessons.title: Types and functions

steps.headline: Rust has whole-number types and decimal types, and dividing one whole number by another gives a whole number.

lead.text: Every value in a Rust program has a **type**, which says what kind of value it is and therefore what can be done with it. Numbers come in two families that are used constantly. The whole numbers, written with no decimal point, have types such as **i32**, a 32-bit integer that holds any whole number from about −2 billion to +2 billion, and the numbers with a decimal point have types such as **f64**, a 64-bit floating-point number. When you write a number and nothing else in the program says which type it has, Rust chooses i32 for a whole number and f64 for a number with a decimal point.

The distinction matters most for division. When both numbers are whole, the result is whole as well: Rust divides, discards the remainder and keeps the quotient, so 9 / 4 is 2 and not 2.25. Writing both numbers with a decimal point, as in 9.0 / 4.0, makes them f64 values, and the division keeps its fraction.

afterFigure.text: The figure prints both results side by side. The whole-number result is not 2.25 rounded: the remainder is simply dropped, so that 9 / 4 and 11 / 4 both give 2. A decimal point therefore changes the answer and not merely its appearance, because **9 and 9.0 are values of different types**.

lead.text: The program below shares 7 between 2 with whole numbers, so the .5 is discarded. What it needs is a different type of number, and not a different calculation.

reveal.text: Only the numbers changed. The name, the division and the println! stayed as they were, because the type of the result follows from the types of the numbers divided.

lead.text: A type can be written after a variable's name with a colon, as in price: f64, and the program below does this for both of its variables. One holds a decimal number and the other a whole number, and the last line multiplies them. Decide whether rustc accepts that.

reveal.text: Rust leaves the conversion to you, because a silent change between whole and decimal numbers could alter a result without leaving any sign in the code. The next screen shows the one word that makes the conversion explicit.

outcome.diagnostics:
error[E0277]: cannot multiply `f64` by `i32`
 --> main.rs:4:26
  |
4 |     println!("{}", price * count);
  |                          ^ no implementation for `f64 * i32`
  |
  = help: the trait `Mul<i32>` is not implemented for `f64`
help: the following other types implement trait `Mul<Rhs>`
 --> /rustc/01f6ddf7588f42ae2d7eb0a2f21d44e8e96674cf/library/core/src/ops/arith.rs:361:1
  |
  = note: `&f64` implements `Mul<f64>`
  |
  = note: `&f64` implements `Mul`
  |
  = note: `f64` implements `Mul<&f64>`
  |
  = note: `f64` implements `Mul`
  = note: this error originates in the macro `mul_impl` (in Nightly builds, run with -Z macro-backtrace for more info)

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0277`.

steps.headline: The word as converts a value from one number type to another.

lead.text: To combine a whole number with a decimal one, you convert one of them, and the word **as** does so: total as f64 takes the whole number held in total and produces the same number as an f64. The variable total is unchanged, since as makes a converted value and does not alter its source, and the new value can then be used in any calculation that needs an f64.

In the figure the whole number 9 is converted before the division, which is why the result keeps its fraction. The conversion belongs to total alone, because as binds more tightly than /: the line is read as (total as f64) / 2.0, a decimal divided by a decimal, and no mixing is left for the compiler to object to.

afterFigure.text: Conversion in the other direction is also possible, but it can lose something. Writing 9.7 as i32 gives 9, because the part after the decimal point is discarded and not rounded, whereas converting a whole number to f64 keeps its value. **The word as marks the place in a program where you decide which of these you want.**

lead.text: Here is the failing program again. Rust accepts the multiplication once both sides have the same type, so the exercise is to convert the right one of them and nothing else.

steps.headline: A function names a calculation, states the types it takes and returns, and gives back its last expression.

lead.text: The programs so far have contained one function, main. You write others with the same word fn, followed by a name, a list of **parameters** in brackets, and an arrow and a **return type** before the braces. In fn double(n: i32) -> i32, the function double takes one parameter, n, which must be an i32, and the arrow says that it hands back an i32. Every parameter and the result have their types written out in this way, because Rust does not guess the types at the edges of a function.

The body is the code between the braces, and the value that the function returns is simply its last line, written *without* a semicolon. In the figure that line is n * 2, so double(21) is 42, and main stores the value in result before printing it. A function is called by writing its name with the values to use for its parameters, and each call runs the body again with the parameters set to those values.

afterFigure.text: The first line of a function can be read as a contract: it says what must be supplied and what will come back, and the compiler checks every call against it. A call that supplies an f64 to double, or that treats its result as text, is rejected before the program runs, which is the same strictness about types as on the earlier screens.

lead.text: Read the first line of a function before its body, because it already states what goes in and what comes out.

reveal.text: Both parameters here are i32 as well, which makes the answer easy to confuse with theirs, but a function could equally take two i32 values and return an f64.

lead.text: Now write a function yourself. Its first line is given, and the body needs a single expression as its last line.
A function can be called more than once, and each call starts afresh with its own value for price. Work out what the two calls hand back and what the program prints.

reveal.text: The same body served two different prices. That is the purpose of a parameter: the calculation is written once, each call supplies its own value, and nothing has to be copied.

lead.text: Here is double again, with one change: a semicolon after n * 2. Decide whether rustc accepts this version.

reveal.text: A semicolon turns an expression into a *statement*, which is carried out and produces no value, so the body ends without an i32 to return. rustc reports that it expected an i32 and found (), the empty value, points at the semicolon and suggests removing it.

outcome.diagnostics:
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> main.rs:1:22
  |
1 | fn double(n: i32) -> i32 {
  |    ------            ^^^ expected `i32`, found `()`
  |    |
  |    implicitly returns `()` as its body has no tail or `return` expression
2 |     n * 2;
  |          - help: remove this semicolon to return this value

error: aborting due to 1 previous error

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0308`.

lead.text: Finally, combine the pieces: a function whose parameters and result are all decimals, and whose body must add before it divides.

reveal.text: The brackets make the addition happen first. Without them, a + b / 2.0 would divide only b by 2.0 and then add a, which is a different calculation.

lessons.orientation: Choose between whole and decimal numbers, and write functions that take and return typed values.
lessons.nextAction: Write your own programs in the Rust projects.

blocks.text: Here is another short program: seven cookies are shared between two people, and the last line prints the result of dividing the one number by the other. On a calculator the quotient would be 3.5, and in Rust what is printed depends on something that the program never states outright, which is the *kind* of number that cookies and people hold.

That makes the kind of a number part of what a program means, and Rust keeps track of it more strictly than most languages do. This lesson covers the two families of number you will use first, whole numbers and decimals, the rule that stops them being mixed carelessly, and the function, which gives a calculation a name, inputs of stated kinds and a result of a stated kind.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose between whole and decimal numbers, and write a function that takes and returns typed values.

recap.keyIdea: Rust keeps whole numbers and decimals apart, and a function returns its last expression, so a semicolon there turns the result into nothing.

blocks.text: Rust treats whole numbers (**i32**) and decimals (**f64**) as different types, so 9 / 4 is 2 while 9.0 / 4.0 is 2.25, and a calculation that mixes the two is rejected until one side is converted with **as**. A function states the types it takes and the type it returns, and what it returns is its last expression, which is why a semicolon at the end of that line leaves the function with no value.
Together with printing, variables and mut from the previous lesson, these are the pieces that most small Rust programs are built from, and the Rust projects ask you to use them side by side.

questions.prompt: What number does this program print?
hints: apples holds 3 and pears holds 4.
The program prints apples + pears.
Add the two values.
questions.onCorrect: 7. Rust added apples and pears before printing, and the braces received the sum.

questions.prompt: Change the program so that it prints 5 and 2.
hints: The braces fill in the order of the values after the text.
Swap the 2 and the 5 after the comma.
questions.onCorrect: The braces are filled in the order the values are listed, so swapping the values swaps the output.

questions.prompt: Write a program that prints two lines: Hello, Rust! and then 3 + 4 = 7. Have Rust work out the 7 by putting 3 + 4 after the text.
hints: Each println! prints one line, so you need two of them.
The second one is println!("3 + 4 = {}", 3 + 4);
questions.onCorrect: Two println! calls make two lines, and the {} in the second receives the value of 3 + 4.

questions.prompt: What number does the program print after area =?
hints: Find width and height first.
area is width * height.
Multiply 6 by 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: area is width * height, which is 6 * 4 = 24.

questions.onCorrect: 24. Each let gave a value a name that the later lines could use.

misconceptions.feedback: Adding 6 and 4 gives 10, but area is defined on the third line as width * height, which is 6 * 4.

questions.prompt: Does this program compile?
hints: Look at how score was created, then at line 3.

acceptedIdeas: No. score was made without mut, so it cannot get a new value.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. score was made without mut, so it cannot get a new value.

choices.label: No. score was made without mut, so it cannot get a new value.
No. Every let needs a type such as i32.

questions.onCorrect: rustc stops with error E0384 and ends its message with the repair itself: let mut score.

misconceptions.feedback: The program would print 15 if Rust allowed the change, but line 3 gives score a second value and score was not created to accept one.
Rust works out the type from the 10, so no type has to be written here. The fault is on line 3.

questions.prompt: Fix this program so that it compiles and prints 15. You only need to change one line.
hints: Run it first. rustc's message ends with a suggested fix.
score needs to be allowed to change, which is decided where it is created.
Line 2 becomes let mut score = 10;
questions.onCorrect: let mut score declares up front that score will change, so the assignment on line 3 is allowed.

questions.prompt: Fix this program without using mut: turn each line that changes level into a new let. It should print 7.
hints: Lines 3 and 4 give level a new value, which plain let doesn't allow.
Start each of those two lines with let.
Line 3 becomes let level = level * 3;
questions.onCorrect: Each let made a new level from the one before, without any mut.

questions.prompt: Write a program where count starts at 1 and is doubled three times with count = count * 2. Then print count = 8.
hints: count changes after it is created, so it needs mut.
Print it with println!("count = {count}");

questions.prompt: Which word do you write after let so that a variable can be given a new value later?
hints: It is short for mutable.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: mut: let mut count = 0;

questions.prompt: Does let x = 5; followed by let x = "five"; compile?
hints: Is the second line changing x, or making a new one?

acceptedIdeas: Yes. The second let makes a new x, and a new variable can have a new type.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. The second let makes a new x, and a new variable can have a new type.

choices.label: Yes. The second let makes a new x, and a new variable can have a new type.
No. x is an integer, so it can never hold text.
No. You need let mut x for the second line.

misconceptions.feedback: That would hold if line 2 assigned to the same x, but a second let makes a new variable, which is free to hold text.
mut is needed only to assign to the same variable. A second let creates a new one and needs no permission.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
hints: cookies and people are both whole numbers.
Dividing two whole numbers in Rust gives a whole number.
How many whole times does 2 go into 7?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 7 / 2 with two whole numbers gives 3. The remainder of 1 is dropped.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Dividing two whole numbers gives a whole number, so Rust dropped the remainder of 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the exact quotient, but cookies and people are whole numbers, and Rust keeps only the whole part of their quotient.

questions.prompt: This program prints 3. Change it so that it prints 3.5.
hints: 7 and 2 are i32 values, so the remainder is dropped.
Write both numbers with a decimal point.
questions.onCorrect: 7.0 / 2.0 divides two f64 values, so the .5 is kept.

questions.prompt: Does this program compile?
hints: Look at the two types written after price and count.

acceptedIdeas: No. Rust will not multiply an f64 by an i32 until you convert one of them.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. Rust will not multiply an f64 by an i32 until you convert one of them.

choices.label: No. Rust will not multiply an f64 by an i32 until you convert one of them.

questions.onCorrect: rustc reports E0277: it has no multiplication that takes an f64 and an i32.

misconceptions.feedback: Many languages would convert for you and print 10, but Rust stops and asks you to choose the conversion.
The result would be 10.0 if count were an f64, but Rust does not convert it on its own.

hints: Only the multiplication needs to change.
Write count as f64 where count is used.
questions.onCorrect: count as f64 turned 4 into 4.0, so both sides of the * are f64.

questions.prompt: In fn area(w: i32, h: i32) -> i32, what type does area return?
hints: The return type comes after the arrow.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: i32, the type after the arrow.

questions.onCorrect: i32. The type after the arrow is what the function hands back.

questions.prompt: Write a function triple that takes an i32 and returns three times it, also as an i32.
hints: The body's last line is the value the function returns.
Write n * 3 with no semicolon after it.
questions.onCorrect: n * 3, with no semicolon, is the value that triple returns.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
hints: Work out add_tax(50) and add_tax(20) separately.
price / 10 is integer division: 50 / 10 is 5.
Add 55 and 22.
questions.onCorrect: 77. Each call ran the body with its own price and handed back the last expression.

questions.prompt: Does this version compile?
hints: What does a semicolon do to the last line of a function body?

acceptedIdeas: No. The semicolon turns n * 2 into a statement, so the function returns nothing.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. The semicolon turns n * 2 into a statement, so the function returns nothing.

choices.label: No. The semicolon turns n * 2 into a statement, so the function returns nothing.
No. A function body must use the word return.

questions.onCorrect: rustc reports E0308, mismatched types, and its help line says to remove the semicolon.

misconceptions.feedback: Without the semicolon it would print 42. With it, n * 2 is calculated and then thrown away.
The word return is allowed but not required. The last expression, written without a semicolon, is the return value.

questions.prompt: Write a function average that takes two f64 values and returns their average as an f64.
hints: Add the two values, then divide by 2.0.
Brackets make the addition happen first: (a + b) / 2.0
questions.onCorrect: The brackets add before the division, and f64 keeps the fraction.

questions.prompt: Write total_price, which takes a price as an f64 and a count as an i32, and returns price times count as an f64.
hints: count is an i32, so convert it before multiplying.

questions.prompt: Write share, which splits a whole number of sweets between people and returns how many each person gets. Leftover sweets are not shared out.
hints: Dividing two i32 values already drops the remainder.

questions.prompt: Which type does Rust give 2.5 when nothing else in the program says otherwise?
hints: It is a 64-bit floating-point type.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: f64, Rust's default for numbers with a decimal point.

flashcards.front: In Rust, what must you write to give an existing variable a new value with =?
flashcards.back: Create it with let mut, for example let mut count = 0;

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: let mut

flashcards.front: What is it called when a second let reuses a variable's name?
flashcards.back: Shadowing. The new variable hides the old one and may have a different type.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Shadowing

flashcards.front: In Rust, what does 9 / 2 evaluate to?
flashcards.back: 4. Dividing two integers drops the remainder.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 9 / 2 is 4 with remainder 1, which is dropped.

flashcards.front: A Rust function's last line is x + 1; with a semicolon. Why does the function not return x + 1?
flashcards.back: The semicolon makes it a statement. Only a final expression without a semicolon is returned.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The semicolon turns it into a statement.
